basic_identification.name: Digital fashion / wearable art
basic_identification.originator: DressX (Daria Shapovalova & Natalia Modenova, 2020), RTFKT (Benoit Pagotto & Steven Vasilev, 2020, acquired by Nike 2021), Auroboros (Paula Sello & Alissa Aulbekova), The Fabricant (Kerry Murphy, Amsterdam, 2018), Tribute Brand, Digitalax, Carlings
basic_identification.geography: Global. Key hubs: Los Angeles (DressX), Amsterdam (The Fabricant), London (Auroboros), Portland (RTFKT/Nike). Markets concentrated in US, Europe, with growing Asia-Pacific adoption

core_ideas.core_claim: Clothing can exist as purely digital artifacts — worn via AR filters, in virtual environments, and on avatars — reducing environmental impact by 97% compared to physical production while enabling unlimited creative expression unconstrained by physics, material costs, or manufacturing logistics. Digital fashion expands what 'wearing' means beyond physical bodies.
core_ideas.medium_specificity: Entirely digitally native in its purest form: virtual garments exist as 3D models, AR overlays, and avatar skins with no physical counterpart. The medium specificity includes: physics-defying designs impossible in physical fabric, real-time body tracking for AR try-on, cross-platform avatar compatibility, NFT-based ownership verification, and AI-generated design tools. The 'phygital' hybrid (digital + physical pairs) bridges but does not eliminate the digital specificity.
core_ideas.relation_to_attention_economy: Deeply embedded in attention economy. Digital fashion is inseparable from social media self-presentation — garments are designed to be photographed, shared, and liked. DressX's AR try-on for TikTok and Zoom explicitly serves platform engagement. The practice inherits fashion's attention logic (trend cycles, influencer culture, brand identity) and amplifies it through digital shareability. However, the sustainability argument provides an intention-based counter-narrative.
core_ideas.relation_to_intention: Split. The sustainability intention (97% less carbon, 3,300 liters less water per garment) serves a genuine structural need. The creative intention (unleashing design from physical constraints) serves artistic expression. But the dominant commercial intention is attention capture through novelty, brand extension (Nike/RTFKT), and metaverse positioning. The practice oscillates between genuine innovation and marketing spectacle.

market_economics.revenue_model: Direct sales of digital garments (individual pieces $10-$9,999+), AR filter licensing, NFT primary and secondary sales, brand partnerships and commissions, platform fees, subscription models. Nike/RTFKT generates revenue through phygital drops (NFT + physical redemption). DressX operates as a marketplace with creator fees. The Fabricant creates bespoke digital fashion for luxury brands.
market_economics.market_position: Cross-market: spans primary art/fashion market (original digital garments), NFT secondary market, gaming/metaverse market (avatar skins), and luxury brand extension market. Infrastructure position through platforms (DressX as marketplace, The Fabricant as B2B creation tool).
market_economics.price_range: Wide range: AR filters $1-$30, digital garments $10-$500, limited edition NFT fashion $500-$10,000+, RTFKT collaborations $5,000-$100,000+. Auroboros luxury digital pieces can exceed $10,000. The market is bifurcated between accessible AR fashion and luxury/collector digital fashion. [uncertain]
market_economics.volume_trend_2024_2026: Growing from ~$3 billion (2025) with projected explosive growth (CAGR 167.54% to $55 trillion by 2035 per some estimates, though these projections are speculative). Post-NFT crash, the market pivoted from speculative NFT drops to utility-focused AR fashion and gaming skins. DressX partnered with Google AR Labs in 2024. 21 of top 50 fashion brands have launched NFTs. Growth is real but projections vary wildly. [uncertain]
market_economics.collector_demographics: Gen Z and millennial digital natives (primary market), gaming communities, crypto-adjacent collectors (declining post-crash), luxury fashion enthusiasts exploring digital, fashion industry professionals, metaverse early adopters. The Fabricant attracts fashion industry clients. DressX targets social media content creators. RTFKT targets sneaker culture and gaming crossover audiences. [uncertain]
market_economics.sustainability: Uncertain. The sustainability narrative (environmental benefits of digital vs. physical) provides a durable value proposition independent of hype. AR try-on has practical utility (reducing returns in e-commerce). But the NFT-speculative model proved unsustainable post-crash. Long-term sustainability depends on: AR technology maturation, metaverse adoption (still speculative), integration with gaming platforms, and whether consumers adopt digital wardrobe as routine practice rather than novelty.

practice_aesthetics.toolchain: CLO 3D, Marvelous Designer (3D garment simulation), Blender, ZBrush (3D modeling), Substance Painter (texturing), Unreal Engine, Unity (real-time rendering), AR development kits (ARKit, ARCore, Snap Lens Studio), AI design tools (Stable Diffusion for concept generation), NFT minting platforms (Ethereum, Polygon, Tezos), body tracking/scanning technology. Adobe Creative Suite for 2D design.
practice_aesthetics.relation_to_AI: Increasingly central. AI is used for design generation (RTFKT launched AI-generated sneaker lines), pattern creation, body measurement from photos, virtual try-on improvement, and trend prediction. AI accelerates the design pipeline and lowers barriers to creation. The threat is that AI-generated fashion may commoditize design skill. The opportunity is that AI enables personalization at scale and democratizes fashion design for non-specialists.
practice_aesthetics.liveness: Mixed. AR try-on is real-time and interactive. Avatar fashion is persistent but customizable. NFT drops are event-based with temporal scarcity. Some pieces are generative (responding to music, movement, or environmental data — Auroboros's music-reactive outfit). The practice spans the full spectrum from static digital objects to real-time responsive garments.
practice_aesthetics.aesthetic_vocabulary: Borrowed from both fashion and digital art, still forming its own. Terms include: phygital, digital twin, virtual try-on, skin, avatar wearable, AR fashion, metawear, digital couture, crypto fashion. The vocabulary often defaults to fashion terminology (collection, drop, season) or tech terminology (minting, rendering, AR). A distinctive critical vocabulary for evaluating digital fashion as art (beyond novelty or sustainability) is underdeveloped.
practice_aesthetics.tendency_axis_position: Tends toward enclosure (brand-controlled, platform-specific), capture (social media optimization, trend-driven), spectacle (novelty and visual impact over critical depth), and individual (personal expression, self-presentation). Some commons elements exist (DressX as open marketplace, The Fabricant's educational programs) but the dominant tendency is commercial and brand-driven.

infrastructure_governance.openness: Mostly proprietary. Brand designs are IP-protected. Platforms (DressX, The Fabricant) are centralized. RTFKT/Nike operates under corporate IP. Some open-source 3D tools exist (Blender) but the fashion-specific toolchain is largely proprietary. Limited open standards for digital garment interoperability.
infrastructure_governance.governance_model: Corporate. DressX is a venture-backed startup. RTFKT is Nike-owned. The Fabricant is a VC-funded company. Auroboros is a luxury brand. No DAO governance despite NFT roots. Decision-making is founder/corporate-driven. The fashion industry's hierarchical brand model dominates over crypto's decentralization ethos.
infrastructure_governance.data_sovereignty: Limited. Users of AR try-on generate body data that platforms collect. NFT ownership provides some asset sovereignty (tokens on public blockchains). But platform-dependent garments (AR filters) disappear if the platform closes. DressX controls its marketplace data. The Fabricant controls B2B client data. Cross-platform portability is promised but rarely delivered.
infrastructure_governance.interoperability: Low but improving. Tribute Brand claims cross-platform compatibility (Decentraland, Fortnite, Sandbox simultaneously). OpenMetaverse and Khronos Group (glTF standard) are working on 3D asset interoperability. But most digital garments are platform-locked: an AR filter for Instagram does not work on TikTok; a Fortnite skin does not transfer to Decentraland. True interoperability remains aspirational.
infrastructure_governance.preservation_strategy: On-chain metadata for NFT fashion provides some permanence. But the visual assets (3D models, textures) are typically stored on IPFS or centralized servers — vulnerable to loss. AR filters depend on platform maintenance. No institutional preservation infrastructure for digital fashion. The practice is at risk of significant loss as platforms evolve and early works become incompatible with current systems.
infrastructure_governance.consent_architecture: Minimal. AR try-on requires camera access (binary consent). NFT purchases imply consent to blockchain transparency. Body scanning data collection follows standard app privacy policies. No granular consent for how body data is used, stored, or shared. No machine-readable consent protocols. The practice inherits the fashion industry's loose relationship with consent and the tech industry's surveillance model.

field_position.relation_to_traditional_art_world: Parallel to the art world, integrated with the fashion world. Digital fashion appears at fashion weeks (Auroboros at London Fashion Week), technology conferences, and NFT events more than at art galleries or museums. Some crossover into art contexts (Museum of the Moving Image, V&A) when framed as 'wearable art.' The practice challenges art-world boundaries by operating in fashion, gaming, and tech simultaneously.
field_position.what_it_enables: Creative expression unconstrained by physical materials, gravity, or manufacturing. Dramatic reduction in fashion's environmental footprint. New revenue streams for designers without physical production infrastructure. Body-positive design (digital garments fit any body). Global distribution without shipping. New forms of identity expression in virtual spaces.
field_position.what_it_lacks: Tactile experience — you cannot feel digital fabric. Interoperability across platforms. Stable business models post-NFT crash. Critical discourse that evaluates digital fashion as art rather than novelty or sustainability claim. Physical craft traditions that ground fashion design. Clear regulatory frameworks for virtual goods ownership. A compelling reason for mainstream consumers to pay for clothes they cannot physically touch.
field_position.who_is_excluded: Those without smartphones or AR-capable devices. Communities without reliable internet. Older demographics unfamiliar with AR/virtual environments. Those who value tactile, material experience in clothing. Traditional fashion workers whose skills (sewing, pattern-making, textile knowledge) are devalued. Global South producers who depend on physical garment manufacturing employment. Consumers who cannot afford the hardware required for full digital fashion engagement. [uncertain]
field_position.frontier_signal: Frontier practice, still emerging. The concept is established but mainstream adoption remains uncertain. AR try-on is reaching product-market fit. Gaming skins are a proven market. But 'digital-only clothing' as a consumer category is still experimental. The frontier is in: AI-personalized fashion, haptic feedback garments, brain-computer interface fashion, and seamless cross-platform digital wardrobes.

attention_intention.discovery_mechanism: Social media (Instagram, TikTok — core discovery channels), fashion media, tech media, NFT platforms, influencer marketing, brand partnerships (Nike drives RTFKT discovery), fashion week coverage, gaming platforms. Algorithm-driven discovery is dominant.
attention_intention.attention_dependency: Very high. Digital fashion exists to be seen and shared. Without social media, the primary use case (AR fashion for photos/video) largely disappears. The practice is structurally dependent on visual social platforms. Gaming skins are less platform-dependent but still require active online communities.
attention_intention.intention_alignment: Primarily attention-native in current form. The sustainability intention is real but secondary to the commercial attention-capture model. The artistic intention exists but is subordinated to brand-building and market positioning. The practice would need to develop utility-first models (replacing physical samples, reducing waste in production) to become more intention-aligned.
attention_intention.commons_contribution: Low. Proprietary designs, closed platforms, limited open-source contribution. Some educational content (The Fabricant's workshops). DressX provides marketplace access for independent designers, which has commons-adjacent effects. But the practice predominantly encloses rather than shares.

provenance_temporality.provenance_type: Ownership provenance via NFTs/blockchain (for NFT fashion). Standard brand attribution for non-NFT digital garments. No meaning provenance — the practice does not track how the significance of garments changes over time. The blockchain provides transparent ownership history but limited contextual provenance.
provenance_temporality.temporal_logic: Cyclical (fashion seasons, trend cycles, collection drops) and event-based (limited drops, collaborations). AR fashion is present-tense (worn and discarded). NFT fashion has blockchain permanence but cultural ephemerality. The temporal logic inherits fashion's planned obsolescence rather than art's durational ambitions.
provenance_temporality.absence_handling: The practice identifies certain absences: the absence of sustainable fashion (and offers digital as solution), the absence of body-diverse design (digital solves sizing), the absence of creative freedom in physical constraints. But it does not address the absence of tactile experience, craft tradition, or critical discourse within its own practice.

coherence.coherence_vs_consensus: Neither strong coherence nor consensus. The field is fragmented between luxury digital fashion, mass-market AR, gaming skins, NFT collectibles, and sustainability-focused practice. No shared framework for evaluation or quality. The fashion industry's trend logic prevents stable coherence. Each brand maintains its own vision without field-level dialogue.
coherence.contestability: Low within brands (corporate direction). Moderate in public discourse (sustainability claims are contested, NFT value is debated). The crypto community contests platform control. Fashion critics contest whether digital fashion is fashion. Art critics contest whether it is art. But no formal contestation mechanisms exist.
coherence.forkability: Moderate. Individual designers can create digital garments with accessible tools (Blender, CLO 3D). But forking a platform (DressX) or brand (RTFKT) requires significant capital and network effects. The tools are forkable; the market position is not.

adai_comparison.what_adai_should_adopt: The cross-industry thinking — digital fashion refuses to stay within art-world boundaries, operating simultaneously in fashion, gaming, tech, and sustainability. This boundary-crossing is relevant to A(DAI)'s ambition to map the full digital arts field. The sustainability argument demonstrates how digital practices can serve structural needs beyond aesthetic ones. DressX's marketplace model offers lessons in platform design for creative communities.
adai_comparison.what_adai_should_refuse: The attention-capture business model that subordinates all other values to social media virality. The planned obsolescence logic inherited from fashion. The weak consent architecture for body data. The interoperability gap between promise (open metaverse) and reality (platform lock-in). The sustainability greenwashing risk when environmental claims are not independently verified.
adai_comparison.structural_tension: Digital fashion demonstrates that digital art practices can achieve mass adoption and commercial sustainability — but through attention economy mechanisms A(DAI) explicitly resists. The tension is between reach (digital fashion reaches millions) and depth (A(DAI) seeks structural intelligence over surface engagement). Can A(DAI) achieve the boundary-crossing reach without the attention dependency?

regulatory_legal.regulatory_exposure: Growing. Virtual goods face consumer protection questions (what do you own?). NFT fashion faces securities regulation uncertainty. AR try-on faces biometric data regulations (Illinois BIPA, GDPR). Digital garments as virtual goods may face VAT/tax treatment questions. No specific digital fashion regulation exists yet, but multiple regulatory domains apply. EU Digital Services Act may affect platform marketplaces.
regulatory_legal.ip_model: Brand-controlled, all rights reserved. Designs are protected by copyright and, in some cases, design patents. NFTs provide proof of ownership but IP remains with the creator/brand. Licensing agreements govern use in specific platforms. Open-source fashion design is rare. The IP model follows fashion industry norms: strong brand protection, limited consumer rights to modify or resell.
regulatory_legal.opt_in_vs_opt_out: Opt-in for purchases and platform use. Implicit opt-in for data collection through app usage. No opt-out for data harvesting within platforms. Blockchain transactions are transparent by default (no opt-out from public transaction history). The practice defaults to tech industry opt-out norms rather than developing consent-forward models.

ecosystem.platform_dependency: High. AR fashion depends on smartphone platforms (iOS, Android) and social media platforms (Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat). NFT fashion depends on blockchain infrastructure (Ethereum, Polygon). Metaverse fashion depends on specific virtual platforms (Decentraland, Fortnite, Roblox). DressX is a single point of failure for its marketplace ecosystem. Nike's support is critical for RTFKT. Multiple platform dependencies create fragility.
ecosystem.network_effects: Strong. More users create more demand for digital garments, attracting more designers, creating more content. DressX benefits from marketplace network effects. Gaming platforms benefit from skin ecosystems. However, platform fragmentation limits cross-platform network effects. Each platform's network effects are siloed.
ecosystem.post_crash_trajectory: Pivoting post-2022-2023 crash. NFT fashion speculation collapsed. RTFKT's NFT drops declined in value. The field pivoted toward: utility-focused AR (DressX + Google AR Labs 2024), gaming integration (Fortnite, Roblox skins), brand extension (Nike using RTFKT for phygital products), and sustainability marketing. The speculative phase ended; the utility phase is beginning. Growing but from a reset baseline.
